newsitem.title: USA: Rubin implies stronger yen wish-economist Bergsten.
newsitem.headline: Rubin implies stronger yen wish-economist Bergsten.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury was implicitly calling for a stronger Japanese yen by its recent comments highlighting Japan's trade surplus, U.S. economist Fred Bergsten said Wednesday.
"Now it's our Treasury, not our trade office, going after Japan," Bergsten, the director of the Institute for International Economics, told CNBC television.

"They are going after its aggregate trade surplus - not specific sectors - and that means the responses have to be broad economic changes, like a stronger exchange rate for the yen which I would say our Treasury, at least implicitly, is now calling for."

Bergsten said strong statements over the last month or two from Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and his deputy Lawrence Summers had emphasized U.S. concern that the Japanese trade surplus should not become the defining imbalance in the world economy.

The Japanese trade surplus was the largest in the world and Japan was the biggest creditor in the world. Conversely, the United States trade deficit is exceeding $200 billion annually and was the biggest debtor country in the world.
"On those fundamentals it is quite clear that the yen is too weak, the dollar is too strong. On those fundamentals the yen has clearly got to strengthen quite considerably."
Bergsten said the strong U.S. economy and rising interest rates was good insurance against the dollar falling too far too fast.
"That in a way provides a cushion to try and get an orderly readjustment to avoid building up these big trade problems in the future," he said.
Rubin sets off for Asia on Thursday on a six-day trip that includes a meeting with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Tokyo on Friday.
